info.bio:
The New York Dolls es un grupo de música rock formado en Nueva York en 1971.
Consiguieron poco éxito durante su vida, pero los New York Dolls ejemplificaron lo que vendría poco después en la era de punk rock e incluso más tarde; las influencias de su estilo travestido y exagerado se notan en la apariencia de muchos grupos de hair metal. Su estilo musical descuidado, pero altamente energético marcó la pauta para muchas bandas de rock and roll posteriores.

scenes.name: Lite metal: pop metal y glam
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El subgénero que, desde 1983-84, intensifica el polo melódico del heavy y lo mezcla con el hard rock, quitándole el grave grueso. Philip Bashe lo llamó «metal pop» y señaló a Def Leppard y Van Halen; otros ejemplos son Poison, Bon Jovi, Ratt y Cinderella. Sus detractores, el público tradicional y el del thrash, lo llaman «poseurs», «false metal», «nerf metal», «poodle bands» o «glam», motes que describen bien sus rasgos: falta de autenticidad, pelo cardado, ropa colorida en lugar del negro obrero. Voz dulce sin gruñidos, armonías al modo de Aerosmith y Kiss, letras de amor y lujuria con nombres de chica y, sobre todo, la power ballad, que entra en radios que excluían el heavy y gana público nuevo, como las versiones blancas de Pat Boone en los cincuenta. MTV impulsó mucho su desarrollo. Se queda con la herencia dionisíaca y elimina el caos: «lo realmente pesado se quita».

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.

podcast.title: Life-Changing Influence (1973)
podcast.body: A New York Dolls concert in 1973 had a profound, life-changing impact on Cristiuala (Poison Ivy) and Gilsher (Lux Interior), inspiring them to seek out and consume "anything that was sexy, wild, and played rock and roll." "Veren con cierto a New York Doll, ese mismo año les cambió la vida."

podcast.body: While their last shows were in 1976 and they were definitively done by October 1977, an arbitrary breakup date of October 1, 1977, is assigned due to the difficulty in pinpointing the exact end. "So we'll just have to assign an arbitrary date of October 1st, 1977 for the breakup."

podcast.title: Members in Sid Vicious's New York Band – September 1978
podcast.body: Sid Vicious formed a new band in New York in September 1978, which included two musicians who were formerly members of the New York Dolls. "He had a band together, consisting of two guys from the New York Dolls and Mick Jones of the Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Johnny Thunders' Death (1991)
podcast.body: Guitarist Johnny Thunders died of a drug overdose in New Orleans on April 23, 1991, with some people maintaining there were conspiracy theories suggesting he was murdered. "After hitting Miss Solar career, guitarist Johnny Thunders died of a drug overdose in New Orleans on April 23rd of 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Jerry Nolan's Death (1992)
podcast.body: Drummer Jerry Nolan died on January 14, 1992, from a stroke that followed a severe case of bacterial meningitis, spending his final weeks on a respirator. "And finally, drummer Jerry Nolan died of a stroke following a bad case of bacterial meningitis on January 14th, 1992."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Arthur Kane's Sudden Death Post-Reunion (2004)
podcast.body: Just 22 days after returning to Los Angeles from the reunion gig in England, Arthur Kane felt ill, was diagnosed with leukemia in an emergency room, and died within two hours. "But just 22 days after returning to LA from England, Arthur felt like he had the flu. He went to an emergency room of an LA hospital where he was diagnosed with leukemia. And within two hours, two hours, he was dead, just like that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Morrissey Curates Reunion at Meltdown Festival (2004)
podcast.body: In 2004, Morrissey was invited to curate England's Meltdown Festival and used this opportunity to fulfill a personal dream by reuniting his favorite band, the New York Dolls. "In 2004, Morrissey was asked to curate a music festival in England called the Meltdown Festival, knowing that this was his opportunity to make a personal dream come true. He made it his mission to reunite his favorite band of all time, and he did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Reunion Gig and Documentary (2004)
podcast.body: The three surviving members—David Johansen, Sylvain Sylvain, and Arthur Kane—regrouped, rehearsed, and played a reunion gig on June 16, 2004, an event largely chronicled in the documentary "New York Doll." "The three surviving members of the group, David Johansson, Sylvain Sylvain and Arthur Cain regrouped. And much of what happened is chronicled in a great documentary called New York Doll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: David Johansen Death (2025) – Stage 4 Brain Cancer at 75
podcast.body: David Johansen, charismatic frontman of proto-punk pioneers New York Dolls, died at age 75. He had been diagnosed with stage 4 brain cancer and was also facing costly surgeries for a back fracture. After the Dolls dissolved, he adopted the persona of Buster Poindexter. "Diagnosed with stage 4 brain cancer and facing costly surgeries for a back fracture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arthur Kane's Difficult Post-Breakup Life
podcast.body: Bassist Arthur Kane faced severe challenges after the breakup, moving to Los Angeles where he struggled with alcoholism, experienced a near-fatal fall from a window, and was beaten senseless with a baseball bat by a homeless man, leaving him in a coma; he later became a Mormon in 1989 and worked as a librarian in the church's genealogy center. "Bassist Arthur Kane had a rough time. He moved to Los Angeles where he drank himself into an alcoholic stupor. He was so drunk one time that he fell out of a window, and nearly died."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Carrying On as a Duo
podcast.body: Following Arthur Kane's death, the remaining two Dolls, David Johansen and Sylvain Sylvain, decided to continue as a duo, recording a "pretty good record" titled "One Day, it will please us to remember even this," which included guest appearances by Iggy Pop and Michael Stipe. "This left us with just two dolls. David Johansson and Sylvain Sylvain. They decided to carry on and record an album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Commercial Failure and Impact
podcast.body: Despite being a commercial failure and eventually breaking up due to drugs and alcohol after only two albums, The New York Dolls served a crucial purpose. Their outrageous image, bad attitude, and amateurish playing acted as a catalyst, initiating a unification of "musical weirdos" in New York. "Although the New York dolls were a commercial failure and were eventually torn apart by drugs and alcohol after just two albums, they served a very real purpose."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim vs. Financial Struggle
podcast.body: Despite receiving extensive press, coverage, and praise, the band struggled financially, largely due to significant drug issues. "Lots of press, lots of ink, lots of praise, but not a lot of money. Besides, they had so many drug issues that, well, let's just say that it wasn't pretty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Cult Following and Influences
podcast.body: Despite being dismissed by many for their unconventional style, the New York Dolls developed a significant following among those who appreciated "weird things." They were seen by some as embodying the true spirit of rock and roll, where attitude and energy surpassed virtuosity. The band regularly played alongside other influential artists like Iggy Pop and KISS. "Soon, the dolls were playing regular gigs alongside Iggy Pop, and a band who took the makeup thing even further."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Johansen's Post-Breakup Career
podcast.body: After the breakup, singer David Johansen pursued a solo career, recording under the name Buster Point Dexter, acting in Hollywood, and hosting a show for VH1. "Singer David Johansson went solo, recording some stuff under the name Buster Point Dexter. He did some acting in Hollywood and hosted a show for VH1."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Demise of the Band
podcast.body: After a couple of tours under Malcolm McLaren's management, the band began to fall apart. By March 1975, while on the road in Florida, the Dolls were nearing their end, as evidenced by surviving live recordings from that period. Shortly after this, the band was "done." "Short time later, they were done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early "New Wave" Designation
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, some writers began to refer to The New York Dolls as "new wave" or "a new wave in rock," applying the term to artists who rejected the traditional norms of blues-based rock and roll. "some writers began referring to groups like the Velvet Underground and the New York dolls as new wave, or at least a new wave in rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Early Influence
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were identified as one of the "ultra-fringy players" in the early 1970s whose music was outside the mainstream and only for "weirdos" at the time, but retrospectively recognized as incredibly important to the history of alternative rock. "People like Iggy Pop and Lou Reed and The New York Dolls... in retrospect, these are incredibly important people to our story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early New Wave Description
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, critics began using the term "New Wave" to describe artsy, non-mainstream bands like the New York Dolls. "Then some critics started using it in the very early 70s to describe artsy non-mainstream bands like the New York dolls and the Velvet Underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Early Performances at Mercer Art Center (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: The New York Dolls, considered one of the "most important of all the pre-punk bands," played some of their very first gigs at the Mercer Art Center in the early 1970s. This venue was a crucial hub for New York's "outrageous weird stuff" before its collapse in 1973. "The New York Dolls, one of the most important of all the pre-punk bands, along with the Ramones, were known to play some of their very first gigs at the Mercer Art Center."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

podcast.title: Early Spandex Wearers
podcast.body: In 1971, the New York Dolls, a significant pre-punk band, created a sensation in New York City by being the first rock band to perform on stage while wearing spandex. This fashion choice was groundbreaking and contributed to their distinctive image. "back in 1971, the New York Dolls, one of the most important of all the pre-punk bands, created a stir in New York City by being the first rock band to wear spandex on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Featured in Punk Magazine
podcast.body: The fanzine "Punk," which appeared at the end of 1975, covered The New York Dolls, among other raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s and artists in the burgeoning CBGB scene. "It also covered Iggy Pop and the Stooges, The New York Dolls, and even some of their raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s like Question Mark and Mysterians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Naming
podcast.body: The band formed in the fall of 1971, comprising four former teenage gang members from Brooklyn who found playing in a band more appealing than petty burglaries. They took their name from the New York Doll Hospital, a real store on Jamaica Avenue in Queens specializing in doll repairs. "So taking their name from the New York Doll Hospital, which was a real store on Jamaica Avenue in Queens that specialized in fixing rare dolls, the New York Dolls began scary people in Manhattan in the spring of 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heroin Decimation
podcast.body: Heroin tragically decimated and brought death to the band members of The New York Dolls. "Heroin decimated and brought death to the New York dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were a significant part of the underground music scene in Manhattan that captivated Legs McNeill. An unreleased song by the band even provided the initial inspiration for the name of McNeill's first fanzine, "Teenage News," before it was renamed "Punk." "The inspiration for the name came from an unreleased New York Doll song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Punk
podcast.body: The New York Dolls are mentioned as one of the bands that significantly influenced punk, highlighting their role in the pre-punk landscape that Malcolm McLaren was involved with. "Malcolm claren, que nabía sido representante de los New York Dolls, otra de las mandas que acabaron influyendo al punk."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Inspired by Marc Bolan and T-Rex
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were significantly inspired by Marc Bolan's character and the albums of T-Rex. It is considered impossible to fully grasp the artistic and musical essence of late 1970s and 1980s rock, including bands like the New York Dolls, without recognizing the foundational influence of Bolan and T-Rex. "de los New York Dolls, es muy difícil entender el rock de final de los 70 y de los 80. Tanto a nivel artístico, como incluso a nivel musical, sin entender lo que fue el personaje de Marvolan y de lo que fueron estos iscos de T-Rex."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: London Show and Drummer's Death
podcast.body: In November 1972, Rod Stewart invited the New York Dolls to London to open a show for him. During this trip, drummer Billy Mercier became intoxicated, and after being taken back to an apartment by two groupies, he was dunked in cold water in a bathtub and had coffee poured down his throat, leading to his suffocation and drowning. "But then drummer Billy Mercier got drunk. Two groupies hauled them back to their apartment, dunked them in cold water in the bathtub, and poured coffee down his throat. He suffocated and he drowned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longest Hiatus Record (Almost 27 Years)
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were apart for almost 27 years, making them one of the bands with the longest gaps between breakup and reunion, surpassed only by The Stooges. "The dolls were a part for almost 27 years, but we can go one further."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Association
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren, who was at one time their manager, started using the term "new wave" to describe cool new bands that weren't quite punk. "Malcolm McLaren, a one-time manager of the New York dolls, started throwing at the term when he was trying to describe cool new bands that weren't quite punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Management
podcast.body: After being dropped from their record deal, the band hired Malcolm McLaren, the inexperienced but ambitious owner of a small, unusual clothing shop in London, as their new manager. McLaren, who discovered the Dolls during a New York clothing show, envisioned a complete image makeover, replacing their spandex, makeup, and big hair with red leather. He also proposed using a big Soviet flag as a stage backdrop for live performances, a move deemed not particularly smart at the time and less engaging than their previous sexual weirdness. "He thought the dolls needed a complete image makeover. That would fix everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Prior Management
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren, who later formed the Sex Pistols, was the failed manager of the New York band The New York Dolls prior to his venture with the Sex Pistols in 1975. "In 1975, Malcolm McLaren was the failed manager of a New York band called The New York Dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Managed by Malcolm McLaren
podcast.body: Malcolm McLaren served as one of the early managers for the New York Dolls during his time in New York. This role put him in a position to encounter the nascent punk scene and Richard Hell's aesthetic. "Uno de los primeros managers que tuvieron en el malcomma claren que era británico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Members in Sid Vicious's Solo Band
podcast.body: After the Sex Pistols, when Sid Vicious attempted a solo career in New York, a band was put together for him that featured "a few members of the New York dolls." "A band was put together featuring a few members of the New York dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Sid Vicious and Questions About the Murder of Nancy Spungen

podcast.title: Mercer Arts Center Performance
podcast.body: The New York Dolls played at the Mercer Arts Center, which was part of the Broadway Central Hotel and served as a hangout for "weirdos" before its collapse in August 1974. "The New York Dolls played there, and it had become something of a hangout for these weirdos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Morrissey's Inspiration
podcast.body: Stephen Patrick Morrissey, who would later become a prominent musician, was a young Manchester poet wannabe and a fan of the New York Dolls. "Still in Manchester, a group soon to be called Joy Division was inspired by a sex pistols show. Many earliest beginnings of the pet shop boys could be traced to what singer Neil Tennant saw and felt at a single pistols concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Philosophy
podcast.body: The band's music was characterized by short and raunchy songs, deliberately avoiding solos and complex arrangements. They prioritized attitude and energy over musical virtuosity, believing these qualities were more important than technical accomplishment. This approach was a reaction against the increasing sophistication of mainstream rock. "And as for the music, all the songs were short and raunchy. No solos, no complex arrangements."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneers of Makeup and Spandex on Stage
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were notable as the first group to incorporate makeup and spandex into their stage attire. While they never explicitly discussed their sexuality, they were content to let audiences draw their own conclusions, contributing to an ambiguous and liberated image. "They never spoke with their sexuality, but we're only too happy to let people make assumptions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Pioneers of Over-the-Top Glam Makeup
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were notable for their adoption of over-the-top glam makeup styles during the early 1970s, contributing to the flamboyant visual aesthetic of the era. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Precursors to Punk Rock
podcast.body: The New York Dolls were an extremely important band of the pre-punk era in New York, predating iconic groups like the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and The Ramones, and were instrumental in sparking the punk rock explosion in New York in the mid-1970s. "This very important band of the pre-punk era in New York, spent 26 years, 9 months and one day apart. This group predated the Sex Pistols, the Clash. They were even around before the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Predecessor to The Heartbreakers
podcast.body: Johnny Thunders, who was previously known as Johnny Volum, was a member of the New York Dolls before moving on to form The Heartbreakers. "Thunders had been a part of the New York dolls, but had now moved on to a group called The Heartbreakers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Provocative Image and Early Gigs
podcast.body: The New York Dolls started performing in Manhattan in the spring of 1972, with their first gig at a sleazy hotel in Times Square. They created a shocking image by wearing makeup, spandex, and fishnets, and professing to be gay or bisexual. This look pushed the emerging glam rock aesthetic from London "miles further," distinguishing them significantly. "They showed up wearing makeup, and dressed in spandex, and fishnets, and professing to be gay."

xref.title: First Show October 17, 1975 – Pre-dates Sex Pistols and The Clash; 1980 Ontario Place Riot
xref.body: Teenage Head formed in Hamilton, Ontario, and played their first show on October 17, 1975 at Westdale High School — three weeks before the Sex Pistols played their first gig, and nine months before The Clash formed. They were a major force in Canadian punk, combining elements of the Ramones, New York Dolls, and 1950s rock and roll. Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

xref.title: Formation and Johnny Rotten's Audition (1975)
xref.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren, the former manager of The New York Dolls and co-proprietor of the "Sex" clothing shop at 430 King's Road in London's Chelsea area, sought to form a band as a living advertisement for his store. He liked the name "Pistols" for its dangerous connotation, thus "Sex Pistols." Malcolm was looking for a singer and was introduced to 19-year-old Johnny Lydon (later Johnny Rotten), who had green teeth and was spotted by Bernie Rhodes wearing a homemade "I hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt held together with safety pins. Despite Lydon's inability to sing, Malcolm had him audition by miming and "singing" Alice Cooper's "I'm 18" to a jukebox in the shop, which landed him the role. "So Malcolm got young John to audition, not caring if Johnny could actually sing a note, which he couldn't."

xref.title: Murder at Chelsea Hotel (October 12, 1978)
xref.body: Nancy Spungen, girlfriend of Sid Vicious, was found dead from a single stab wound to her stomach in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Nancy had a troubled life, diagnosed with schizophrenia at 15 and supporting herself through prostitution from age 17 before becoming a groupie to bands like The Ramones, New York Dolls, and Aerosmith. She became inseparable from Sid Vicious for 19 months, and they both were heroin and Tuinal addicts. On the night of October 11, 1978, several people visited their room, and Sid allegedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, completely incapacitating him. At around 2:30 am on October 12th, Nancy asked Rockets Redglare, their drug connection and Sid's bodyguard, for Dilaudid. Later, around 7:30 am, female moans were heard, and at 10 am, Sid called the front desk. Nancy was found stabbed and bleeding to death, in a weird angle under the bathroom sink. Sid initially confessed but was likely too incapacitated. The theory later emerged that Rockets Redglare, who died in 2007, was the murderer, allegedly stabbing Nancy with Sid's Bowie knife during an argument over stolen cash, a confession he reportedly made while drinking at CBGB. "Nancy Spungin, girlfriend of ex-sex Bristol Sidvicious, at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978."

xref.title: Commercial Failure and Impact
xref.body: Despite being a commercial failure and eventually breaking up due to drugs and alcohol after only two albums, The New York Dolls served a crucial purpose. Their outrageous image, bad attitude, and amateurish playing acted as a catalyst, initiating a unification of "musical weirdos" in New York. "Although the New York dolls were a commercial failure and were eventually torn apart by drugs and alcohol after just two albums, they served a very real purpose."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cult Following and Influences
xref.body: Despite being dismissed by many for their unconventional style, the New York Dolls developed a significant following among those who appreciated "weird things." They were seen by some as embodying the true spirit of rock and roll, where attitude and energy surpassed virtuosity. The band regularly played alongside other influential artists like Iggy Pop and KISS. "Soon, the dolls were playing regular gigs alongside Iggy Pop, and a band who took the makeup thing even further."

xref.title: Evolution from Hardcore to Power Pop
xref.body: The Replacements initially started as a hardcore act, heavily influenced by punk bands like the Ramones, Sex Pistols, and New York Dolls. Over time, they became more melodic and adopted more conventional song structures, influenced by The Rolling Stones, The Beatles, and CCR, eventually evolving into a power pop band. "They recorded for a label called Twin Tone and were very much a hardcore-acted first. Their heroes were the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and the New York Dolls. But as things went on, they became more melodic and their songs had more conventional structures thanks to their love for the Rolling Stones and the Beatles and CCR. Leader Paul Westorberg grew into a very accomplished songwriter and the longer the bands stayed together, the more they became a power pop band."

xref.title: New York Dolls Management
xref.body: Malcolm McLaren, owner of a "small, weird clothing shop in London," ventured into band management after encountering the New York Dolls during a clothing show in New York. When the Dolls were dropped from their record deal and sought new management, McLaren, despite his inexperience, stepped in with ambitious plans. He envisioned a radical image makeover for the band, proposing red leather attire instead of their previous spandex and makeup, and using a large Soviet flag as a live backdrop, a move that proved to be less appealing to their original fanbase. "His name was Malcolm McLaren, and he chanced upon the dolls when he was in New York for a clothing show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York Dolls and Band Management
xref.body: After a trip to a New York fashion fair in 1973, Malcolm McLaren became deeply interested in the New York Dolls and decided to try his hand at band management. This initial venture was a disaster, and the Dolls soon broke up, but McLaren remained undeterred.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Over-the-Top Glam Makeup
xref.body: In the early 1970s, David Bowie was a proponent of over-the-top glam makeup styles, which were characteristic of the era and his artistic expression. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of Makeup and Spandex on Stage
xref.body: The New York Dolls were notable as the first group to incorporate makeup and spandex into their stage attire. While they never explicitly discussed their sexuality, they were content to let audiences draw their own conclusions, contributing to an ambiguous and liberated image. "They never spoke with their sexuality, but we're only too happy to let people make assumptions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Pioneers of Over-the-Top Glam Makeup
xref.body: The New York Dolls were notable for their adoption of over-the-top glam makeup styles during the early 1970s, contributing to the flamboyant visual aesthetic of the era. "Styles run from the over-the-top glam of David Bowie and the New York Dolls in the early 1970s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Dolls Plans
xref.body: After the New York Dolls ultimately fell apart following a couple of tours under his management, Malcolm McLaren returned to England. He carried with him "definite ideas on what he'd do next time," suggesting his experience with the Dolls significantly shaped his future endeavors in the music industry. "But all was not lost. Because Malcolm McLaren went back to his shop in England with some definite ideas on what he'd do next time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Precursors to Punk Rock
xref.body: The New York Dolls were an extremely important band of the pre-punk era in New York, predating iconic groups like the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and The Ramones, and were instrumental in sparking the punk rock explosion in New York in the mid-1970s. "This very important band of the pre-punk era in New York, spent 26 years, 9 months and one day apart. This group predated the Sex Pistols, the Clash. They were even around before the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

xref.title: Predecessor to The Heartbreakers
xref.body: Johnny Thunders, who was previously known as Johnny Volum, was a member of the New York Dolls before moving on to form The Heartbreakers. "Thunders had been a part of the New York dolls, but had now moved on to a group called The Heartbreakers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Provocative Image and Early Gigs
xref.body: The New York Dolls started performing in Manhattan in the spring of 1972, with their first gig at a sleazy hotel in Times Square. They created a shocking image by wearing makeup, spandex, and fishnets, and professing to be gay or bisexual. This look pushed the emerging glam rock aesthetic from London "miles further," distinguishing them significantly. "They showed up wearing makeup, and dressed in spandex, and fishnets, and professing to be gay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reunion Gap - 26 Years, Eight Months, 16 Days
xref.body: Taking October 1, 1977, as the breakup date and June 16, 2004, as the reunion gig date, the New York Dolls experienced a hiatus of 26 years, eight months, and 16 days. "So if we take October 1st, 1977, as the break-up date, then we have a hiatus of 26 years, eight months, and 16 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

xref.title: Spandex and Makeup Style
xref.body: The New York Dolls were notable for their "Spandex and makeup wearing" style, emblematic of the glitter rock movement that found a home in America. "the Spandex and makeup wearing New York dolls."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Stephen Patrick Morrissey's Fanaticism
xref.body: The legend of the New York Dolls grew to "mythic proportions," captivating Stephen Patrick Morrissey (singer for The Smiths) from a young age, who wrote letters to British music magazines praising them and founded their British fan club. "One of their biggest all-time fans was Stephen Patrick Morrissey. Yes, the same guy who sang for the Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unreleased Song "Teenaged News"
xref.body: The fanzine "Punk" was initially intended to be named "Teenaged News," after an unreleased song by The New York Dolls, before they found inspiration for their final title. "Now at first, this fanzine was supposed to be called Teenaged News, after an unreleased song by The New York Dolls."
